questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Sap concentration as water leaves a cell
questions.learningObjective: State what happens to sap concentration as water leaves a cell
questions.stem: A translator's note flags the phrase sap becomes concentrated as water leaves it; the translator must confirm what actually changes in the cell.

options.text: The sap becomes more concentrated as water leaves by osmosis, so solute potential falls.
The sap becomes diluted as water leaves, because lost water carries solute with it.
options.misconception: thinks water leaving carries solute away

options.text: The sap concentration is unchanged, because water leaves by pumping with no solute movement.
options.misconception: assumes water loss happens without moving any water

options.text: The sap concentration falls, because water leaves and takes dissolved solute away with it.
options.misconception: confuses dilution with concentration of the sap

questions.explanation: As water leaves a cell by osmosis, the remaining solute is concentrated and its solute potential becomes more negative. Dilution, unchanged concentration and solute loss all contradict osmosis.
questions.hint: Losing water from a fixed solute load concentrates it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the forces that hold a water column together under tension
questions.stem: Another translator's note asks what keeps the water column in a tall xylem conduit from breaking under tension.

options.text: The active pumping of xylem cells, which pushes the column upward with each breath.
options.misconception: mistakes passive transport for active pumping by the plant

options.text: Cohesion between water molecules and their adhesion to the conduit walls.
The rigid lignin in the walls, which pushes the water column upward from below.
options.misconception: treats wall lignin as a pump rather than a support

options.text: Root pressure from the soil, which pushes the column up beyond the plant's height.
options.misconception: overstates the reach of root pressure

questions.explanation: Cohesion holds water molecules together and adhesion anchors them to the wall, so tension at the top transmits down the column. Root pressure cannot reach great heights.
questions.hint: Two forces: molecules clinging to each other, and to walls.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a sequence of water potentials from soil to leaf
questions.stem: A translator's note tabulates water potential at three points on a plant: soil -0.2 MPa, root -0.4 MPa, leaf -1.0 MPa; what does the sequence show?

options.text: A gradient from more negative to less negative potential, which drives water downward.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the water potential gradient

options.text: No gradient, because the three values are so close together to matter for flow.
options.misconception: ignores a gradient because the values differ only slightly

options.text: A gradient from less negative to more negative potential, which drives water upward.
A gradient of zero, because soil and leaf potentials balance each other out.
options.misconception: assumes the soil and leaf values cancel to zero

questions.explanation: Water moves from higher to lower water potential, so -0.2 to -1.0 MPa is the gradient pulling water from soil to leaf. Reversing the sign destroys it.
questions.hint: Water travels from higher potential toward lower potential.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Name the fault produced when a gas bubble blocks a xylem conduit
questions.stem: One translator's note sketches a conduit in which an air bubble has blocked the narrow tube; name the fault.

options.text: Coalescence, where the bubble has merged with sugar in the adjacent sieve tube.
options.misconception: confuses an air blockage with a sugar process

options.text: Flocculation, where particles of clay from the soil have settled in the tube.
options.misconception: describes soil particles rather than a gas bubble

options.text: Guttation, where water has been pushed out of the tube and lost to the air.
options.misconception: confuses an internal bubble with water loss at the surface

options.text: Cavitation, where a gas bubble interrupts the continuous water column.

questions.explanation: An air bubble breaking the continuous water column in a conduit is cavitation, and it stops flow through that vessel. Coalescence, clay settling and guttation are other processes.
questions.hint: A gas bubble in a water column is the giveaway.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct an account of root pressure as the main lifting force
questions.stem: A translator's note claims a tapped tree bleeds sap because root pressure pushes water out of the cut; identify the flaw in that account.

options.text: Root pressure is weak and cannot raise water to the height of a tall canopy.
Root pressure is strong but stops working once the stem is cut open.
options.misconception: believes cutting the stem abolishes root pressure

options.text: The flaw is that sap only leaves a cut when the tree is actively photosynthesising.
options.misconception: ties sap bleeding to photosynthesis rather than pressure

options.text: The flaw is that bleeding from a cut is driven by the phloem, not the xylem.
options.misconception: misattributes the bleeding to the phloem

questions.explanation: Root pressure is too weak to push water to the top of a tall plant and works poorly under transpiration. Tapping also damages phloem, so the simple pressure account is incomplete.
questions.hint: Root pressure is a minor force, not the main lift.

questions.stem: A translator's note reports a potted plant losing 30 grams of water in one hour from a leaf area of 100 square centimetres; what was the transpiration rate in grams per square metre per hour?
questions.explanation: One hundred square centimetres is 0.01 square metre, so 30 grams over that area is 3000 grams per square metre per hour. Reading the figure per square centimetre would give the wrong scale.
questions.hint: Convert square centimetres to square metres first.

questions.stem: A translator's note gives 18 grams of carbon gained and 900 grams of water lost in a day; what is the water use efficiency in grams of water per gram of carbon gained?
questions.explanation: Water use efficiency is water lost divided by carbon gained, so 900 divided by 18 gives 50 grams of water per gram of carbon. Inverting the ratio or mixing up the numerator gives the wrong efficiency.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define a source and a sink tissue in terms of sugar balance
questions.stem: A written prompt asks the translator to explain what makes a plant tissue a source or a sink for sugars.

answer.exemplar: A source is a tissue that makes more sugar than it uses, so it exports the surplus through the phloem. A sink is a tissue that consumes or stores more sugar than it makes, so it receives sugar from sources. Mature leaves and storage roots are typical sources, while growing buds, young leaves and developing fruits are typical sinks, and a tissue can change from sink to source as it matures.

questions.explanation: The answer must define both terms by the balance between sugar made and sugar used, with fitting examples. Listing organs without that balance mislabels the tissues.
questions.hint: Source makes more than it uses; sink uses more.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Sap concentration as water leaves a cell
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment showing sap concentration changes as water is lost
questions.stem: A translator's note asks the team to design an experiment showing that a cell's sap concentrates as it loses water.

answer.exemplar: Place a strip of dialysis tubing or a plant tissue cylinder in a solution of known solute concentration, then measure its mass at the start and after thirty minutes on a balance, alongside a control piece in pure water. Repeat at several surrounding solute concentrations and plot final mass change against the external concentration. Tissues in concentrated solutions should lose mass and their sap should concentrate, while tissues gaining mass should show dilution.

questions.explanation: The design needs measured mass change, a control and a range of concentrations, with concentration inferred from water movement. Without a control, drying confounds osmosis.
questions.hint: Weigh before and after, with a control in pure water.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Combine a reach-of-pull question with a property-of-water question
questions.stem: A translator's note considers how far a column of water could be pulled upward by transpiration alone, and which property makes that possible.

options.text: Only a few centimetres, because water cannot resist being pulled.
options.misconception: ignores that water resists tension very strongly

options.text: Very far, because cohesion and adhesion transmit tension down the column.
Only to the root, because the pull stops where the soil ends.
options.misconception: believes transpiration cannot act above the root

options.text: Very far, because the walls of the vessel actively pump the water.
options.misconception: mistakes passive tension for active pumping by walls

questions.explanation: Cohesion between molecules and adhesion to the walls let tension travel along the column, so transpiration can pull water to great heights. No pump works in the vessel.
questions.hint: Tension travels along the column because molecules hold on.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how transpiration creates a pull rather than a push
questions.stem: The note asks why transpiration from the leaves creates a pull rather than simply pushing water up.

options.text: Evaporation creates suction that draws water upward without any change in potential.
options.misconception: describes suction without any potential change

options.text: The stomata actively pump water vapour out, which pulls the column along with it.
options.misconception: treats stomata as active pumps of vapour

options.text: Evaporation from mesophyll cell walls lowers water potential, pulling the column up.
Solar heating of the stem expands the water there, pushing it upward as a thermosiphon.
options.misconception: mistakes thermal expansion for a transpiration pull

questions.explanation: Evaporation from wet cell walls lowers the water potential of the leaf, so water is pulled up the xylem along a potential gradient. Stomata do not pump vapour.
questions.hint: Lower potential in the leaf, higher potential below.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the condition that lets dissolved gas form a bubble in a conduit
questions.stem: A translator's note identifies what promotes the formation of a gas bubble that interrupts a xylem conduit.

options.text: A rise in temperature inside the conduit, which expands the dissolved gas until it escapes.
options.misconception: blames heating rather than a pressure drop below vapour

options.text: A build-up of minerals in the conduit, which precipitates out as solid plugs.
options.misconception: mistakes dissolved gas for mineral precipitation

options.text: An increase in transpiration, which pulls air in through the leaf and down the vessel.
options.misconception: claims increased transpiration pulls air into the vessel

options.text: A drop in pressure below the bubble's vapour pressure, which lets dissolved gas come out.

questions.explanation: When pressure falls below the vapour pressure of dissolved gas, it comes out of solution and forms a bubble that stops flow. Heating and mineral deposits are not the mechanism.
questions.hint: Gas leaves solution when pressure drops too far.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain weak root pressure in humid conditions
questions.stem: A translator's note observes a plant in a sealed chamber with a wet soil still showed only weak root pressure; why is that expected?

options.text: Low humidity limits transpiration, so little tension develops and the pressure stays weak.
Wet soil removes the air from the root zone, so water cannot be drawn in at all.
options.misconception: claims saturated soil blocks water entry completely

options.text: The sealed chamber raises the temperature, which weakens the xylem conduits directly.
options.misconception: blames chamber temperature for the weak pressure

options.text: Weak root pressure always means the plant is dead and cannot transport water.
options.misconception: equates weak root pressure with a dead plant

questions.explanation: Root pressure depends on water entering faster than transpiration removes it, and high humidity cuts transpiration nearly to nothing. Saturated soil and chamber heat do not explain it.
questions.hint: Wet air means almost no transpiration pull develops.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the shape of a cumulative water loss graph
questions.stem: A translator's note plots cumulative water loss from a potted plant against time; what does the shape of that graph show?

options.text: A curve that levels off, because the plant stops transpiring once the soil dries.
options.misconception: assumes transpiration stops once the soil dries slightly

options.text: A horizontal line, because water loss from a potted plant is always negligible.
options.misconception: claims potted plants lose essentially no water

options.text: An almost straight rising line, since transpiration proceeds at a roughly constant rate.
A curve that rises then falls, because stomata close completely at midday.
options.misconception: assumes stomatal closure always stops the water loss curve

questions.explanation: Under steady light, temperature and soil moisture, transpiration runs at a steady rate, so cumulative loss plots as a near-straight line. Flattening needs a change such as drying soil.
questions.hint: Steady conditions give a steady rate of loss.

questions.learningObjective: Find an inverted ratio in a water use efficiency calculation
questions.stem: A translator's note computes water use efficiency by dividing carbon gained by water lost; find the error in that calculation.

options.misconception: blames unit choice instead of the inverted ratio

options.text: The ratio is fine, but both measurements must be taken at the same hour of day.
options.misconception: insists on identical timing rather than a correct ratio

options.text: The ratio is inverted; efficiency is water lost divided by carbon gained.
The ratio is fine, but only the water taken up should be counted, not the water lost.
options.misconception: confuses water uptake with water lost in efficiency

questions.explanation: Efficiency reports water spent per unit of carbon gained, so water lost is divided by carbon gained. Inverting the ratio, changing units or swapping uptake for loss give wrong figures.
questions.hint: Efficiency asks how much water per gram of carbon.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how transpiration pulls water to the top of a tall tree
questions.stem: A translator's note requests a written explanation of how transpiration can pull water to the top of a tall tree.

answer.exemplar: Evaporation from the moist walls of mesophyll cells lowers the water potential inside the leaf, so the xylem sap in the leaf is under tension. Because water molecules cohere to one another and adhere to the lignified conduit walls, that tension is transmitted down the continuous column rather than pulling the column apart. Water is therefore drawn upward from the soil through the roots, the stem and finally into the leaf.

questions.explanation: The answer must link evaporation, lowered leaf potential, cohesion, adhesion and a continuous column to upward movement. Leaving out cohesion or a broken column leaves the mechanism incomplete.
questions.hint: Evaporation creates the pull; cohesion carries it down.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment measuring the effect of humidity on water loss
questions.stem: The team is asked to design an experiment that measures how air humidity affects water loss from a plant.

answer.exemplar: Place identical potted plants in four sealed transparent chambers held at the same temperature and light, but with different relative humidities produced by different amounts of water and salt. Weigh each potted plant at the start and again after a fixed interval, keeping the soil moisture constant by watering to a set weight each time. Plot the mass loss per hour against humidity; loss should fall as humidity rises because the leaf air is closer to saturation.

questions.explanation: It needs controlled temperature and light, a range of humidities, constant soil moisture and mass loss over time. Changing several variables would hide the humidity effect.
questions.hint: Vary humidity only, and keep everything else fixed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of one bubble on flow and on neighbouring conduits
questions.stem: A translator's note considers what happens to the flow in a vessel after a bubble forms, and what a second bubble nearby would cause.

options.text: Flow continues unchanged, since the bubble is lighter than the water around it.
options.misconception: thinks an air bubble leaves the water path intact

options.text: Flow reverses, since the bubble pushes the column down toward the roots.
options.misconception: claims a bubble reverses the direction of flow

options.text: Flow slows slightly, but the conduit keeps working around the obstruction.
options.misconception: understates the effect of a gas blockage

options.text: Flow in that vessel stops, and another bubble extends the damage along the conduit.

questions.explanation: A bubble breaks the continuous column in that conduit, so water can no longer pass through, and more bubbles extend the interruption along the vessel. Flow does not continue, reverse or merely slow.
questions.hint: An air break means water cannot pass at all.

options.misconception: says the pressure is generated above the roots

questions.explanation: Root pressure is generated in the root and is too weak to push water to great heights, so transpiration pull does the main work. It is not confined to non-transpiring plants, nor produced in the stem.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a gas bubble forms in a conduit and stops the flow
questions.stem: A translator's note seeks a written explanation of how a gas bubble can form inside a xylem conduit and stop the flow.

answer.exemplar: Water in a xylem conduit holds dissolved gases in solution because the surrounding pressure keeps them dissolved. If the pressure inside the conduit falls below the vapour pressure of those dissolved gases, they come out of solution and form a bubble. The bubble occupies part of the conduit and interrupts the continuous column of water, so water can no longer pass along that vessel and the embolism spreads if other bubbles form nearby.

questions.explanation: The answer must link dissolved gas, a fall in pressure, bubble formation and the break in the water column. A reply that stops at bubbles forming never explains why the flow stops.
questions.hint: Dissolved gas comes out of solution when pressure drops.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment showing that root pressure is a weak force
questions.stem: A study asks the team to design an experiment that shows root pressure is a weak force.

answer.exemplar: Use two tall plants of the same species, one about two metres and one about ten metres, with the shoot tops cut cleanly. Keep both in warm, humid, well-watered soil so transpiration is low and root pressure is the main driver. If the taller plant shows little or no bleeding while the shorter one bleeds noticeably, the force is insufficient to raise sap to great heights, which is the defining weakness of root pressure.

questions.explanation: The design compares a short and a tall plant under conditions favouring root pressure, then measures the bleeding. Confusing transpiration pull with root pressure would not test the weakness.
questions.hint: Compare bleeding in a short plant and a tall one.

It falls, because the lost water carried some solute out of the cell.

questions.explanation: The solute is unchanged while the sap volume falls from 100 to 98 microlitres, so the concentration rises slightly. Losing solvent always concentrates what remains.

options.text: Root pressure pushes the column up, and the bubble marks where it has broken.

questions.explanation: The upward arrow on a tensioned column is the cohesion-tension mechanism: transpiration pulls while cohesion and adhesion hold it together. Heating and wall pumping do not move the water.

questions.explanation: Transpiration lowers leaf water potential below the soil value, and that difference drives flow; the two never equalise while water moves. An open pipe and equalising gradients are both wrong models.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transpiration rate from a measured loss
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a transpiration rate is obtained by weighing a potted plant
questions.stem: An instruction asks the translator to explain in writing how a measured transpiration rate is obtained from a potted plant.

answer.exemplar: A potted plant with a known leaf area is weighed at the start of a period and weighed again at the end, with the soil surface covered to stop water evaporating from the compost. The difference in mass is the water lost by transpiration over the interval. Dividing that mass by the elapsed time and by the leaf area gives the transpiration rate in grams per square metre per hour, and a known-area leaf can be traced beforehand to supply the divisor.

questions.explanation: The answer must describe weighing, covering the soil, the time interval and the leaf-area divisor that turn a mass loss into a rate. Omitting the soil cover lets evaporation distort the measurement.
questions.hint: Weigh, cover the soil, divide by time and area.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water use efficiency from two measurements
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of water use efficiency under wet and dry watering
questions.stem: An investigation asks the team to design a comparison of water use efficiency between a wet and a dry treatment.

answer.exemplar: Grow two identical sets of plants, watering one group to field capacity and keeping the other on a schedule that allows the soil to dry between irrigations, with both groups given the same light and nutrients. Measure the mass of water supplied to each group, the mass lost by transpiration, and the final dry mass gained by each plant over the same number of weeks. Efficiency is the water used per gram of dry matter produced, which can then be compared between the two treatments.

questions.explanation: The design needs identical plants, a defined watering difference, matched light and nutrients, and measures of both water used and biomass gained. One quantity gives no efficiency.
questions.hint: You need both water used and growth gained.

questions.explanation: Mature leaves make more sugar than they use, so they are the source, and the growing tuber is the sink. Stems conduct sugar rather than exporting it.

options.misconception: thinks concentrated solute raises the water potential

options.misconception: insists solute potential depends only on temperature

options.text: Zero, since the added solute exactly cancels the effect of the solvent.
options.misconception: confuses solute potential with pressure potential

questions.explanation: A more concentrated sap has a lower chemical potential for water, so its solute potential becomes more negative. Concentration, not temperature, drives that change.

options.text: It keeps the conduit narrow, so the sap travels faster through it.
options.misconception: assumes adhesion is about flow speed

questions.explanation: Adhesion between water and the lignified wall helps the wall resist the tension inside the conduit, which would otherwise pull it inwards. It does not seal end walls.
questions.hint: It stops the thin wall being pulled inwards.

options.misconception: blames soil drying though the soil value was unchanged

options.text: The leaf made more sugar, which lowered the potential in the leaf.

The xylem filled with minerals, which lowered the potential in the leaf.
options.misconception: blames mineral accumulation in the xylem

questions.explanation: Because the soil value was unchanged, the drop in leaf potential came from greater transpiration into drier air. Sugar production and minerals do not pull it down like this.
questions.hint: The soil stayed put, so the change came from the leaf.

questions.learningObjective: Name the outcome when tension exceeds the vapour pressure of dissolved gas

options.text: The sap reverses direction, pushing water back down toward the roots instead.
options.misconception: claims a bubble reverses the flow direction

options.text: The conduit seals itself with a gum that blocks the bubble completely.
options.misconception: assumes the plant can seal a bubble with gum

options.text: The water boils briefly, then condenses back into a continuous column.
options.misconception: claims the sap simply boils and condenses back

options.text: A gas bubble forms, the conduit embolises, and water flow through it stops.

questions.explanation: When tension drops below the vapour pressure of dissolved gas, that gas bubbles out, the conduit embolises and flow stops. Reversal, self-sealing and boiling back into a column do not occur.
questions.hint: Gas comes out of solution and the vessel is blocked.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sink tissue receives sugar from a source
questions.stem: A translator's note outlines a written explanation of how a sink tissue receives sugar from a source.

answer.exemplar: Sugar is loaded into the phloem at the source, where sucrose is moved from the mesophyll into the sieve tubes by active transport. This lowers the water potential inside the tube, so water enters osmotically from the xylem and raises the hydrostatic pressure at the source end. The pressure gradient then drives bulk flow of sap along the tube toward the sink, where sugar is unloaded and the water returns to the xylem.

questions.explanation: The answer must link source loading, water entry, a pressure gradient and movement to the sink, with unloading at the far end. Simple diffusion misses the pressure step.
questions.hint: Loading, water entry, pressure difference, then unloading.

questions.topic: Sap concentration as water leaves a cell
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of sap concentration in turgid and wilting leaves
questions.stem: A separate study asks the team to design an experiment showing that the sap of a wilting leaf is more concentrated than that of a turgid leaf.

answer.exemplar: Take matched leaves from the same plant, keeping one fully hydrated and allowing the other to lose water until it visibly wilts. Squeeze a fixed volume of sap from each with a press, then measure the solute concentration of the two samples with a refractometer, or compare the mass of sap evaporated to dryness from equal volumes. The sample from the wilted leaf should give the higher reading, confirming that losing water concentrates the sap.

questions.explanation: The design needs matched leaves in two hydration states, equal sample volumes and a concentration measurement on both. Unequal samples or different plants would confound it.
questions.hint: Same leaf type, two hydration states, equal volumes.

options.text: Tension comes from root pressure, and removing the leaf increases it as water is pushed.
options.misconception: credits root pressure for the tension

options.text: Tension comes from transpiration pull, and removing the leaf relaxes it as the column re-forms.
Tension comes from osmotic entry, and removing the leaf has no effect on it at all.
options.misconception: claims the leaf has no influence on the column

options.text: Tension comes from the weight of the water above, and removing the leaf doubles it.
options.misconception: treats the column as a hanging weight

questions.explanation: Transpiration from the leaf creates the tension, and removing the leaf stops the pull so the column relaxes. Root pressure, osmosis and the weight of water do not explain it.
questions.hint: The pull comes from the leaf, so removing it relaxes.

questions.stem: A translator's note raises what happens to the water potential gradient in the xylem when transpiration stops.

options.text: The gradient steepens, because the water below rises to meet the stationary column.
options.misconception: thinks the gradient grows once pulling stops

options.text: The gradient disappears, because the pull that created it is no longer applied.
The gradient reverses, because water below pushes back up into the leaf.
options.misconception: claims the gradient reverses when the pull stops

options.text: The gradient stays exactly the same, since the leaf continues to evaporate slowly.
options.misconception: claims the gradient survives without any pull

questions.explanation: The gradient exists only while transpiration pulls water from the leaf, so when it stops the potentials even out and the column becomes static. It neither steepens nor reverses.
questions.hint: No pull means no gradient across the plant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a plant continues to function after one conduit embolises
questions.stem: A translator's note wonders why a conduit that has been embolised can sometimes be bypassed by the plant.

options.text: The bubble dissolves back into the water as soon as the pressure returns to normal.
options.misconception: assumes embolised conduits recover spontaneously

options.text: The conduit re-forms as the walls draw back together under the plant's weight.
options.misconception: assumes vessel walls close the gap by themselves

options.text: Adjacent phloem sieve tubes carry the water upward in place of the xylem.
options.misconception: claims phloem can substitute for the xylem

options.text: Other conduits still carry the flow, so the plant can route water around the blockage.

questions.explanation: Many conduits run in parallel, so if some embolise the others still conduct and flow is reduced rather than stopped. Bubbles do not dissolve away, walls do not reseal, and phloem cannot carry water.
questions.hint: Parallel conduits give the plant a spare route.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the top of a tall tree can wilt while the soil is still wet
questions.stem: A translator's note offers a written explanation of why the top of a tall tree can wilt while the soil is still wet.

answer.exemplar: Water must be pulled up the xylem faster than the root can supply it, and at the very top of a tall tree the tension in the column is greatest because it must also overcome the weight of the water above. If transpiration from the leaves outpaces the rate at which the roots can absorb water, the leaf water potential drops, the leaf cells lose turgor and the leaves wilt even though the soil around the roots is still wet.

questions.explanation: The answer must link the limit of the pulling force with the demand of transpiration and the loss of turgor. Saying the soil was dry, or that water rises only from the roots, misreads the situation.
questions.hint: The pull has a limit, and demand can exceed it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design a method to map the water potential gradient through a plant
questions.stem: An inquiry asks the team to design a way to map the water potential gradient through a plant.

answer.exemplar: Sample tissues from several positions, such as root cortex, lower stem, upper stem, petiole and leaf, using the same technique and at the same time of day. Determine the water potential of each sample with a tensiometer or by comparing it against a series of solutions of known osmotic potential until equilibrium is reached. Plotting the values against distance from the root should show a steady fall in potential toward the leaf, which is the gradient that drives the flow.

questions.explanation: The method needs samples from several positions, one consistent measurement method and a plot against distance. Measuring only leaf and root would not map the gradient.
questions.hint: Sample several heights, use one method, plot the values.
